name: 3DVista
tagline: Desktop software for stitching panoramas and building interactive 360 virtual tours you can host or export anywhere.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Sold as a perpetual desktop license, not a subscription.

verdictSummary: The output of 3DVista is just a static web app: equirectangular images in a WebGL sphere, hotspots that jump between them, a floor plan overlay, some info popups. An agent can one-shot a viewer that handles your own panoramas plus a JSON tour graph, and it will look fine on desktop and phone. What you are not getting in one session is the authoring side: the stitcher that turns bracketed fisheye shots into a clean seamless pano, multi-resolution tiling so a 100MP pano loads without eating 80MB, automatic nadir patching, and the drag-a-hotspot GUI that non-developers actually use. If you already have finished equirectangular JPEGs, the DIY build covers most of the real value. If you are shooting raw with a DSLR and a rotator, the stitching math is the product and you should pay.
coreLoopDIY: Loads your equirectangular panoramas into a WebGL sphere viewer and links them together with clickable hotspots, info popups and a floor plan, driven by a single JSON tour file, then exports as a static folder.
requirements: Your own equirectangular panorama JPEGs, already stitched
Node and a browser that supports WebGL2
Any static host, or just a USB stick for offline delivery
Optional: a tiling script if your panos are over about 8000px wide
whatYouLose: The stitcher: bracketed HDR alignment, control points, blending and nadir patching are genuinely hard and not a weekend build
Multi-resolution tiling and progressive loading, so huge panoramas stay fast on mobile data
A visual editor your client or photographer can use without touching JSON
VR headset mode, guided tours with narration, embedded video hotspots, measurement tools
Offline EXE/APP packaging and the polished default skin that makes tours look professionally made
moatNotes: The real asset is the stitching and tiling pipeline plus a decade of fixing edge cases in how panoramas misbehave. The viewer part is commodity.
whyPeopleStillPay: People paying for 3DVista are usually real estate photographers, museums and training departments who shoot the panoramas themselves and bill clients for the result. For them the perpetual license is a one-time cost against billable work, the stitcher saves hours per shoot, and the offline export means they can hand a tour to a client with no hosting story at all. Nobody in that group wants to maintain a JSON schema at 11pm the night before a delivery. A hobbyist with twenty finished panos from a Ricoh Theta is in a completely different position and should just build the viewer.
notes: Split the product in half: the viewer is a weekend, the stitcher is not.
prompt:
Build a self-contained 360 virtual tour viewer and static site generator. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics.

Stack, non-negotiable: Vite + TypeScript + three.js. No React. Plain DOM for UI. CSS in one stylesheet. Everything runs locally and builds to a static folder.

Project layout:
- tours/demo/tour.json : the tour definition
- tours/demo/panos/*.jpg : equirectangular panoramas (2:1 aspect)
- tours/demo/floorplan.png : optional
- src/ : viewer code

tour.json schema (document it in README):
{ "title": string, "startScene": id, "scenes": [ { "id", "name", "pano": path, "initialYaw", "initialPitch", "initialFov", "hotspots": [ { "type": "link" | "info", "yaw", "pitch", "target"?: sceneId, "title", "body"? } ], "floorplan"?: { "x": 0..1, "y": 0..1 } } ] }

Viewer requirements:
- Equirectangular texture on an inverted sphere, PerspectiveCamera inside it.
- Mouse drag and touch drag to look, wheel and pinch to zoom, clamp pitch to +/- 85 degrees, clamp fov 30 to 100.
- Hotspots as CSS2D-style absolutely positioned DOM markers projected from 3D yaw/pitch, hidden when behind the camera. Link hotspots crossfade to the target scene over 500ms using a second sphere; info hotspots open a small panel.
- Scene list drawer, keyboard arrow look, fullscreen button, loading spinner per scene, preload the panos of adjacent linked scenes.
- Optional floor plan overlay in a corner with a dot per scene and a current-position marker; clicking a dot navigates.
- Deep links: #sceneId in the URL, update on navigation, restore on load.
- Gracefully handle a missing pano file with an inline error instead of a blank screen.

Also write scripts/tile.mjs: a sharp-based CLI that takes a large equirectangular JPEG and emits downscaled 4096px and 2048px versions, and have the viewer pick a size based on window width and devicePixelRatio. Do not attempt cubemap tiling.

Explicitly out of scope: stitching raw or fisheye images, HDR merging, nadir patching, a visual hotspot editor, VR/WebXR, video hotspots, measurement.

Ship: npm run dev for local preview, npm run build producing a dist/ folder that works when opened from a file server or copied to a USB stick, a demo tour with two placeholder panoramas generated procedurally if none are supplied, and a README explaining how to drop in your own images and hand-edit tour.json.
